name: Gareth Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the line lead on the canning line at a soft drinks plant by the river. We fill about 1,500 cans a minute when it's running sweet, mostly lemonade and a fizzy iced tea that's oddly popular. My day is changeovers, chasing jams at the seamer, checking fill weights, and keeping an eye on whoever's new. The best bit is a long clean run where the whole line hums at the same pitch. The worst bit is a seamer jam at 4am with sticky syrup everywhere.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the seamer do, for someone who's never seen one?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's the machine that crimps the lid onto the can so it's sealed. If it's a hair out, you get leakers, and leakers in a pallet of 2,000 cans is a very bad day. I'm known as the seamer whisperer, which my boyfriend Tom finds hilarious, because I can't put up a shelf at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it was oversold, but the bits that work are handy. I use a chatbot now and then to tidy up my shift reports so they don't read like I wrote them at 5am, which I did. I wouldn't post much about it, I'd just shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life carries on, and I'm fine with that. I like my job, the pay is good for this kind of work, and there are three other drinks plants within half an hour if I ever fell out with this one. I'd still want the union to get us a better shift pattern, but that's a different fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much changes. I'd keep putting money aside, we've got about nine months' worth plus a bit in a pension, and I'd keep going for the maintenance technician ticket I've been thinking about for ages. Maybe I'd actually start it this year instead of next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down, because I quite like new toys once someone else has tested them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've been thinking about the maintenance ticket for ages. What's held you back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly it's evenings. Tom marks homework at the kitchen table and I fall asleep on the sofa after a twelve-hour shift. I'd like to be the person who fixes the line, not just the person who notices it's broken, but I'm tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI stayed this small, what would it actually do at your plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning, maybe, working out which flavour to run when so we waste less time on changeovers. Possibly predicting when a bearing is about to go. That would be nice, as long as someone still trusts the old engineer who can hear a bearing going from across the hall.

S0.say: I'd say it was oversold but the useful bits are handy, like tidying my shift reports. I wouldn't post much about it, I'd just shrug.
S0.think: Privately it means my life carries on, and I'm fine with that. I like the job, the pay is good, and there are other drinks plants nearby if I needed them.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving on top of about nine months' cushion and a pension. Possibly starts the maintenance technician course this year instead of next.
S0.feel: Calm, with a small sense of being let down because he enjoys new tools once someone else has tested them.
S0.quote: I'd like to be the person who fixes the line, not just the person who notices it's broken, but I'm tired.
S0.fieldNote: Gareth is comfortable and knows it, and has a long-delayed plan to move into maintenance. Tiredness, not fear, is what stops him. He treats AI as a modest helper and still trusts the old engineer's ear over any sensor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so let's make sure it's done fairly. I'd back the union asking for training on company time before any new kit goes in. Online I'd share the decent stories, the ones where a plant retrained its people instead of sacking them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the canning line is exactly the kind of place it hits. We already have a robot palletiser at the end of the line, and it's brilliant, I'll admit it. If they add vision checks and self-adjusting seamers, the line needs fewer people like me just watching and tweaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the maintenance technician course straight away, the evening one at the college, about two years part time. I'd ask the plant to pay some of it, because they'd want people who can fix the new kit. I'd use the AI tools a bit more at work too, once the engineers showed they actually worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a useful way. Like a kick up the backside I've needed for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your line would struggle most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our quality checker, Pavel. He walks the line with a clipboard and a gauge, and he's brilliant at it, but a camera would do it faster. He's 55 and he's said more than once that he just wants to get to his pension. The robot doesn't need to be better than Pavel, it just needs to be cheaper than Pavel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fair. What would fair look like to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody laid off without first being offered training and a real job at the end of it. And if the plant saves money, some of it goes into wages, not just the shareholders. That's what the union should be fighting for, and I'd turn up to that meeting.

S1.say: I'd say it's happening, so it has to be done fairly. I'd back the union asking for paid training before new kit arrives and share stories of plants that retrained people.
S1.think: Privately, the canning line is exactly where it hits, because fewer people would be needed to watch and tweak. I already admire the robot palletiser at the end of the line.
S1.do: Starts the two-year part-time maintenance technician course at once and asks the plant to cover some of the cost. Uses AI tools more at work once the engineers show they work and backs the union's push for paid training.
S1.feel: Uneasy, but in a useful way, like a long-needed kick to get moving.
S1.quote: The robot doesn't need to be better than Pavel, it just needs to be cheaper than Pavel.
S1.fieldNote: Steady disruption is the push Gareth needs to finally do the course he has postponed. He waits for proof before adopting tools but moves once the case is clear. His sense of fairness is concrete: training before layoffs and a share of savings in wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and somebody needs to slow it down. I'd be signing anything that called for a pause, a robot tax, or money for workers who lose out. At work I'd tell people to get to the union meeting because that's where it'll get sorted, if anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd think I've left it too late. The maintenance ticket wouldn't help if robots fix robots. Two years and I'm 29 with a skill nobody needs, and that's a strange thing to say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the course, honestly, because what's the point. I'd put every spare penny into savings and stop the holidays and the new car we were looking at. I'd get properly involved in the union and in pushing our local politicians for a plan, because I don't think one person can out-plan this. Tom and I would probably sit down and talk about whether we can live on his pay for a while, if teaching even survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. That cold feeling when you realise the plan you were going to start one day doesn't work anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd say, well, I finally found a reason not to do my homework. Then we'd probably both go quiet. He's the one who teaches kids what jobs to want, and he wouldn't know what to tell them either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you wait for proof before changing. Would you wait here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and that's the strange part. Normally I let others go first, but with two years there's no first and second, everyone's in it at once. So I'd do the boring safe stuff fast, savings and the union, and wait on the big decisions because I wouldn't know what they are.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and someone needs to slow it down. I'd sign anything calling for a pause, a robot tax or support for workers, and tell people at work to get to the union meeting.
S2.think: Privately I'd feel I'd left it too late, because a maintenance ticket won't help if robots fix robots. At 29 I'd have a skill nobody needs.
S2.do: Drops the course, saves every spare penny and cancels the holidays and new car. Gets properly involved in the union and in pressing local politicians for a plan, and works out with Tom whether they could live on one wage.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with the cold feeling of a someday plan that no longer works.
S2.quote: He's the one who teaches kids what jobs to want, and he wouldn't know what to tell them either.
S2.fieldNote: His usual habit of waiting for proof breaks down here, because everyone is hit at once. He moves fast on safe steps and freezes on the big ones. The sharpest moment was his line about Tom not knowing what jobs to tell children to want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, let's not waste them arguing about whether it's real. I'd want the government and the companies to set up proper retraining money now. At work I'd be the one nudging people to get their certificates sorted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think five years is enough to get one step ahead but not enough to be safe. I could finish the maintenance ticket and get a couple of years installing and fixing the new robots before they can fix themselves. That might carry me to 32, and then I'd need another idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the maintenance course right away and try to get onto the team that installs the new kit at our plant. I'd save hard, maybe twelve months of expenses instead of nine. I'd learn the AI tools properly, because by then the engineers would have proved they work. Tom and I would hold off on buying a flat until we could see what both our jobs look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy-anxious. Having something to do helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be doing in 2031, if you could pick?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with people, I think. I run the training for new starters on the line, and I'm good at it, they actually remember where the emergency stops are. Maybe the last job is the one where you explain the robots to scared people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want to see pay for the retraining money you mentioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies making the money from it, through tax. I don't think it's fair that we pay for our own courses so a firm can sack us cheaper later. But I'd still do the course with my own money if I had to, I'm not going to sit and wait on principle.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years, so let's not waste them arguing whether it's real. I'd want proper retraining money now and I'd nudge people at work to get their certificates.
S3.think: Privately five years gets me one step ahead but not safe. I could install and fix the new robots for a few years, then I'd need another idea.
S3.do: Starts the maintenance course at once and aims for the team installing new kit at his plant. Builds savings to about twelve months of costs, learns AI tools properly and puts off buying a flat with Tom.
S3.feel: Anxious but busy, with the action itself easing the worry.
S3.quote: Maybe the last job is the one where you explain the robots to scared people.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Gareth a bridge: fixing robots for a while before they fix themselves. He sees his real strength in training new starters, which points to work with people. He holds firm views on who should pay but won't let principle stop him acting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so there's no excuse for anyone being left behind. I'd push for a national retraining plan and for unions to have a say in how robots come in. Online I'd be the calm one in the comments, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years suits someone like me. I don't jump first, but I get there. By the time it's clear what works, I'd still be in my early thirties with time to switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the maintenance course in the first two years, then work on robot installs and keep watching. Around year five I'd look at training or teaching adults, maybe at the college where I did my diploma. I'd keep saving, and Tom and I would probably buy a flat after all, a small one, because ten years of rent is a lot of money gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A bit of background hum, like the line running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still buy a flat. Isn't that a risk if work disappears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and I've thought about it. We'd only borrow what Tom's salary alone could pay, and we'd keep the savings separate. I'd rather owe money on four walls than pay rent for ten years waiting for the end of the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does this picture compare with the fast one for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Night and day. With two years I'd be scrambling and angry, with ten I'd be planning. The end point is the same, which is a bit scary when I say it like that, but the time is what lets someone like me catch up.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly, so no one should be left behind. I'd push for a national retraining plan and a union say in how robots arrive.
S4.think: Privately ten years suits someone like me, who doesn't jump first but gets there. I'd still be in my early thirties when it's clear what works.
S4.do: Takes the maintenance course in the first two years, then works on robot installs while watching. Looks at teaching adults at his old college around year five, keeps saving and buys a small flat with Tom sized to one salary.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with a low background hum of worry.
S4.quote: I'd rather owe money on four walls than pay rent for ten years waiting for the end of the world.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years fits Gareth's steady style, so the same end point feels manageable. His flat purchase is a careful bet sized to one salary. He contrasts scrambling and anger in the fast case with planning here, and he sees time itself as what lets him catch up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. I'm a let-other-people-go-first person, and that picture doesn't let anyone go first. What would help is real money for retraining that you could start straight away, paid for by the companies that gain, and the union having a say in how fast the machines come in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much I actually like my job. People hear canning line and think it's mindless, but I can hear a bad seam before the checker finds it. I'd want whatever comes next to feel like that, like I'm good at something.

headlineQuote: People hear canning line and think it's mindless, but I can hear a bad seam before the checker finds it.
portrait: Gareth Nakamura, 27, is the line lead on a soft drinks canning line, proud of being the seamer whisperer and good at training new starters. He waits for others to test new tools before he uses them, and has long put off a maintenance technician course out of plain tiredness. A plateau leaves him calm, and steady disruption finally pushes him into the course. Fast AGI leaves him alarmed because his late plan no longer works, while five and ten years let him bridge through robot maintenance towards teaching adults. He wants the companies that gain to fund retraining and unions to have a say.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it gives a let-others-go-first person no chance to catch up.
whatWouldHelp: Real retraining money he could start straight away, paid for by the companies that gain, and a union say in how fast machines come in.
